505.title: Nothing is impossible (Luke 1:26–38)
505.hook: Mary asks how, and hears: with God nothing shall be impossible
505.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Annunciation on March 25, nine months before Christmas; Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting, and many Christians read this passage in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, struck silent: Zechariah asked for proof and lost his voice, while Elisabeth kept her joy hidden. Your line was silence can grow things.

In the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy, Luke says, the same angel is sent somewhere completely different. Not the capital, not the holy place, not to a priest. To Nazareth, a village in Galilee the Old Testament never mentions. To a young woman named Mary, engaged to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. Luke doesn't give her age, or say what she was doing. Cooking, maybe. Fetching water. Ordinary hours in an ordinary house. Yesterday an old priest in the temple. Today a young woman in a village nobody's heard of. And her message is far stranger than his.

Gabriel's greeting, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." She's troubled, Luke says, and turns the words over, wondering what kind of greeting this is. Then the news: she will bear a son, name him Jesus, he will be called the Son of the Highest, and his kingdom will have no end. Mary asks: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Notice the difference. Zechariah asked, how can I be sure? Mary asks, how will this happen? Not proof. Just how. Gabriel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee. Then a sign she can go and see: her relative Elisabeth, the one called barren, is six months along. And then: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." The Greek can also be read as no word from God will be without power. And Mary's answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Then the angel leaves. Christians across the churches treasure this scene and honor Mary in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with special devotion as the Mother of God; the Hail Mary prayer opens with Gabriel's greeting. Many Protestant Christians honor her as a model of trusting faith. All of them hear a yes in her last line.
screen: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`
then, large: `WITH GOD NOTHING SHALL BE IMPOSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: Hold something in your life that looks impossible, a relationship beyond repair, an illness, a habit you can't break, someone you love who seems unreachable, honestly, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands; Mary didn't pretend, she asked how. Then loosen your grip a little. If you pray, bring it to God, and if the words fit, say Mary's line: be it unto me according to thy word; if not, hold it open, without forcing an answer.
Gabriel. The angel who told Mary that with God nothing is impossible, and that no word from him lacks power.
Your line: be it unto me. Not whether, but how. Day five hundred five, done.

506.title: He has filled the hungry (Luke 1:39–56)
506.hook: Mary's song turns the world upside down, and Luke's whole gospel will follow it
506.howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said daily in several traditions: at Vespers in the Catholic Church, at Evening Prayer or Evensong in Anglican churches, and at the morning service in Orthodox churches; some Christians also connect it with feeding the hungry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gabriel and Mary's yes: with God nothing shall be impossible. Your line was be it unto me.

Mary doesn't stay home with her news. Luke says she went with haste into the hill country of Judah, to the house of Zechariah, to see Elisabeth, the sign the angel gave her. A young woman, newly pregnant, and an older relative, the one people called barren, now six months along. Two unlikely mothers under one roof. Mary steps through the door and greets her, and the baby inside Elisabeth jumps. Luke says the babe leaped in her womb. Some readers say John, not yet born, is already doing his job: pointing.

Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." And then Mary sings. In the King James Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin the first word is Magnificat, and that's the song's name. It starts personal: God has looked on me, a lowly servant. Then it widens and turns the world upside down: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Mary sings it in the past tense, as if it's already happened. It echoes an older song, sung by Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman who praised God for a child and a world turned over. Luke puts it at the start because his whole Gospel follows this song. Again and again, the poor are lifted and the comfortable unsettled. Later, in Luke's version of his sermon, Jesus says: "Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled." Mary's song is the overture, and the rest of the book plays its tune. Catholic Vespers and Anglican Evensong still sing or say it each evening. Some hear it mostly as God's mercy to the humble heart; others also hear a call to feed the hungry, here and now.
screen: then, large: `HE HATH FILLED THE HUNGRY WITH GOOD THINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of where hunger is close to you: a neighbor living alone, a food bank in your town, a coworker who's broke until payday, someone on the corner you pass every day. Picture one face, and a plate set in front of them, not scraps, good things, the way Mary sang it. If you pray, offer that picture to God as part of Mary's song; if not, let it shape one real thing you'll do.
Magnificat, the name of Mary's song, from its first Latin word, magnify: she sings that God lifts the lowly and fills the hungry with good things.
Your line: the hungry filled. Mary's song, still sung as the day ends. Until tomorrow.

507.title: His name is John (Luke 1:57–80)
507.hook: Zechariah's tongue loosens into a song: the dayspring from on high
507.howItsDone: The Benedictus is sung or said each morning in several traditions: at Lauds in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours and at Morning Prayer in Anglican and Lutheran traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magnificat, Mary's song of the mighty put down. Your line was the hungry filled.

Eight days after the baby is born, the house is full: neighbors, cousins, the whole family, there for the circumcision and the naming. Everyone agrees: name him Zechariah, after his father. Then Elisabeth speaks up: "Not so; but he shall be called John." The relatives push back. Nobody in your family has that name. So they turn to the father, still silent after all these months, and make signs to ask him. And the old priest who couldn't say a word asks for a writing tablet.
screen: `EIGHT DAYS: A HOUSE FULL OF OPINIONS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all." Not his name will be John. His name is John: the angel settled it months ago. In that moment of trust, "his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God." After months of silence, out comes praise, then a song. In Latin it begins Benedictus, blessed: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people." The first half is about all Israel, God keeping old promises to Abraham and David. Then the old man turns to the child, and the song turns tender: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways." Eight days old, and hearing your job description. Then: "whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace." Dayspring is an old English word for sunrise. Christians hear in it Jesus, the light John will point toward. Behind it is the Greek anatole, a rising, and some readers notice the old Greek version of the prophets uses the same word for the promised branch from David's line. A sunrise, and a new shoot from an old tree. In Catholic Lauds and Anglican and Lutheran Morning Prayer, Zechariah's song is still prayed or sung at the hour the dayspring comes.
screen: then, large: `THE DAYSPRING FROM ON HIGH HATH VISITED US.`

segments.voice: If it's morning, face the light; if not, picture tomorrow's sunrise, the sky going gray, then pale, then gold at the edge. Think of the darkness Zechariah sings about, the shadow someone you know, or you, may be sitting in, and let the light come up slowly in your mind, a little at a time. If you pray, greet the morning with Zechariah's words, light to them that sit in darkness; if not, watch the light arrive.
Benedictus. Latin for blessed, the first word of Zechariah's song when his tongue is loosed, still sung in morning prayer.
Your line: the dayspring from on high. Light, a little at a time. That's day five hundred seven.

508.title: In those days (Luke 2:1–7)
508.hook: an emperor counts his people, and God arrives uncounted
508.howItsDone: Luke 2:1–20 is a Christmas reading in churches, and some families read it aloud at home on Christmas Eve or at the Christmas table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Benedictus: Zechariah's tongue loosed into a song of the dayspring. Your line was the dayspring from on high.

Somewhere in Rome, an order goes out: count everyone, so the empire knows who it can tax. It's the kind of thing powerful people do without thinking twice: a line in a decree, and ordinary lives rearranged. Families pack up and go, each to their own city, to be registered. Among them, walking from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, are Joseph, of the house of David, and Mary, the young woman he's engaged to, great with child. The emperor will never hear their names. He's counting heads, not looking at faces.

Luke opens the scene like a history book, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Some readers puzzle over how this census fits other records of the time, and Luke doesn't stop to explain. He cares about the contrast. The emperor's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town, little Bethlehem from Micah, without the emperor ever knowing. Then the birth, in two verses: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No angels yet, no star. A feeding trough for a crib. And notice what isn't there: no innkeeper. Nobody slams a door. Luke's Greek word for inn is the one he uses later for the guestchamber where Jesus eats the Passover with his friends. So some scholars picture a family house with its guest room already full, and the baby laid where the animals fed. The emperor sits at the center of the world, counting. In the Christian telling, God arrives at its edge, uncounted, in a crowded place, in a feeding trough. Some see a hint of the end of Luke's story, when his body is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb hewn in stone.
screen: `THE CENTER COUNTS; GOD COMES TO THE EDGE.`
then, large: `THERE WAS NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Think of the biggest story in today's news, big names, big numbers, and look underneath it for the people at its edges who'll never be named: a family packing up, a nurse on a night shift, a child somewhere in the crowd. Pick one and hold them in mind for a moment, by face, not by number. If you pray, pray for them; if not, simply let them matter to you for a minute.
Kataluma, Luke's Greek word for a guest room, usually translated inn: the opening of his birth story, where an emperor counts the world and Jesus is born at its edge, laid in a manger.
Your line: not counted, but there. Born at the edge, where the animals fed. See you tomorrow.

509.title: Good tidings of great joy (Luke 2:8–20)
509.hook: the angel to the shepherds: fear not, a savior is born
509.tomorrow: now let me go in peace
509.howItsDone: Christians read the shepherds' story at Christmas, and the angels' song lives on in the Gloria, sung or said in Sunday worship in some churches, and in Christmas carols.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kataluma: a full guest room, and a baby laid in a manger at the edge of an emperor's world. Your line was not counted, but there.

Out in the fields near Bethlehem, a few shepherds are keeping watch over their flock by night. It's dark, and the job is mostly staying awake. Not people anyone would invite to a palace. Not people the emperor's census was thinking about. Then, in the King James Bible: "the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid. Terrified. The dark field suddenly blazing. And the angel's first words are ones Zechariah and Mary have already heard.

"Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." Every phrase is loaded. Good tidings means good news, the very thing the word gospel names, coming to shepherds, about a baby. To all people: not just the important ones. This day: tonight, not someday. And the sign isn't a palace or a crown: "Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." The sign is how ordinary he is. Then the sky fills with a multitude of angels praising God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." That line opens the Gloria, a hymn still sung in churches. Compare Bibles and the end of the line varies: the King James says good will toward men; other translations say peace among people with whom God is pleased. Then the shepherds do the simplest thing: "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." They find everything as they were told, spread the word, and people wonder at it. Then a quiet line: "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The shepherds broadcast; Mary treasures. Both are ways of receiving good news. And the shepherds go back to the same sheep, glorifying and praising God as they go.
screen: `THE SIGN IS HOW ORDINARY HE IS.`
then, large: `GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY, TO ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Find one piece of good news that's actually true, a friend's recovery, a kindness you saw, a baby born, a small win, and sit with it for a moment the way Mary pondered. Then picture the person who'd most like to hear it, someone surrounded by bad news lately, and imagine telling them the way the shepherds did, a little breathless, not polished. If you pray, give thanks for it first; if not, simply enjoy it before you share it.
Evangelist. The English word that comes from the angel's own verb, to announce good news, first spoken to shepherds in a dark field.
Your line: great joy for all people. Not just the important ones. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)
510.hook: Simeon holds the child and says he can die content; Mary is told a sword will pierce her soul
510.howItsDone: Christians in many traditions say or sing the Nunc Dimittis at the end of the day, at Compline or Evensong, and many churches keep February 2 as the Presentation of the Lord, also called Candlemas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, evangelist: good tidings for shepherds in a dark field, for all people. Your line was great joy for all people.

Forty days after the birth, Joseph and Mary carry the baby up to the temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked of new parents. Luke tells us their offering: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The law allowed birds instead of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. So this is a poor couple with a newborn, in the crowded temple courts. Nobody pays them attention. Except one man, who has waited a long time for this exact moment, and walks straight toward them.

His name is Simeon. In the King James Bible, he was "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." It had been revealed to him that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Christ. He takes the baby in his arms and sings: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss. The Greek verb is the one used for releasing a servant from duty, or relieving a watchman at the end of his shift. Simeon has stood watch his whole life. Now he's off duty. He calls the child "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Both: the nations and his own people. A surprise: Luke never says Simeon was old. People assume it because he's ready to die, and artists have always painted him with a white beard. The text just says he was waiting. Then he turns to Mary, and the song changes key. This child will cause the fall and rising of many, a sign that people will speak against, and: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also." A warning in the middle of the blessing. Christians have long heard in it the cross, and Mary standing near it. Catholic devotion remembers this as the first of Mary's sorrows. Joy and grief in one embrace, over a poor family's child.
screen: then, large: `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Look back over today and name one good thing your eyes saw: a face, a kindness, a moment of light, even a small one. Then notice what you're still standing watch over, and imagine setting it down for the night, like a watchman going off duty. If you pray, you can say Simeon's words tonight, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace; if not, let the day be finished, and rest.
Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's song, holding the child, ready to go in peace because his eyes have seen.
Your line: depart in peace. Even a watchman gets to go off duty. Day five hundred ten, done.

511.title: Anna, eighty-four (Luke 2:36–40)
511.hook: a widow who never left the temple speaks of the child to all who waited
511.howItsDone: Anna is remembered with Simeon at the feast of the Presentation on February 2 in some churches, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor her as a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nunc dimittis: Simeon, ready to go off duty. Your line was depart in peace.

Some congregations have a woman like this. She's been there longer than anyone. She knows where the spare candles are kept. She was praying in that pew before the current pastor was born. She's buried a husband, maybe more than one friend, and she keeps coming, early, every time the doors open. Visitors walk right past her. And she's often the one who notices when something real is happening. Right after Simeon, in the same temple, Luke introduces her ancient counterpart, in three short verses.

In the King James Bible: "And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser." Aser is Asher, one of the tribes of Israel. And Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, the name of the Hannah whose song echoed in Mary's. She was married only seven years, and then: "she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Fourscore and four is eighty-four. Even in English the line reads two ways: she was eighty-four, or she'd been a widow eighty-four years, which would make her far older. Translations differ. Either way: years of the same faithful routine, in the same place, waiting. Then: "she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem." After all those years, her timing is perfect. Simeon sings and blesses. Anna talks, to everyone who's been waiting like her. In a way she's one of the first people in Luke to tell others about Jesus. Some readers notice Luke pairing a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna. Then the family goes home to Nazareth, and the child grows strong, filled with wisdom, the grace of God upon him. A week crowded with waiting people: Mary's yes, Mary's song, Zechariah's Benedictus, the census, the shepherds, Simeon. And Anna, who never stopped.
